scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: Hello, the partner network feels REALLY slow today from
my machine (pc1) -- getting anything from their side (pc2, 200.1.1.2) takes
ages, though it does eventually respond. Yesterday it was snappy. I don't
understand the connection between our two companies, I'm afraid. Could
someone check why it's so slow today? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I cannot reproduce slowness between pc1 and the partner host pc2. End-to-end latency is low and stable: topology-wide reachability shows pc1→pc2 RTT ≈1.0 ms with 0% loss. Large-MTU pings (1472B payload, DF set) also complete in ≈0.95 ms, ruling out MTU/fragmentation issues. Application responsiveness is immediate: HTTP from pc1 to 200.1.1.2 completes in ~1 ms total time across multiple trials. Throughput is healthy in both directions: iperf from pc1→pc2 averages ~140 Mbit/s and pc2→pc1 ~138 Mbit/s, with minimal retransmits. 

The routing/control plane is normal: BGP between router1 and router2 is Established with prefixes exchanged, and each router’s FIB shows the correct next-hops. Data-plane health looks good: all links are up at full duplex with no duplex or speed mismatches (ethtool shows 10G/Full), and fq_codel is the only qdisc with no backlog or drops recorded. Interface error counters are clean; only a handful of TX-dropped packets are seen on pc1 eth0 (41) and router2 eth1 (19), which is negligible and consistent with transient buffer pressure, not sustained degradation.

Localization: No bottleneck found on router1:eth0/eth1, router2:eth0/eth1, or hosts pc1/pc2. Mechanism-wise, nothing suggests queuing, loss, or control-plane instability that would cause “ages to respond.”

Root cause: No active network-side fault observed; the earlier slowness was likely transient or application/host-related outside the network path.

Corrective fix: No change required. Recommend monitoring; if the issue recurs, capture timestamps with ping/iperf and traceroute from pc1, plus host CPU/load on pc2, to correlate any endpoint or transient congestion events.
